title: Aortic dissection
claims: Stanford A involves the ascending aorta (± arch/descending). Surgical emergency.
Stanford A complications: aortic regurgitation, tamponade, coronary (usually RCA) occlusion, stroke.
Stanford B is distal to the left subclavian artery. Usually medical: IV beta-blocker first (impulse control), then vasodilator.
Stanford B complications: renal or mesenteric malperfusion, limb ischemia, rupture.
Presentation: tearing chest/back pain, BP difference between arms, widened mediastinum on CXR.
Risk factors: hypertension, Marfan/Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid valve, cocaine, trauma.
The aortic wall has three layers: intima (endothelium), media (elastic lamellae and smooth muscle, most of the strength), adventitia.
Cystic medial degeneration weakens the media (Marfan, aging, hypertension).
An intimal tear lets blood enter the media and split the layers, creating a false lumen.
The intimal flap separates true and false lumens and can occlude branch vessels (malperfusion).
